Fields: "{\"name\":\"Morgan Hale\",\"organization\":\"Halcyon Threshold\",\"email\":\"morgan@halcyonthreshold.org\",\"comment\":\"Submitted technical comment FMIR-2026-0042 on Frontier Model Incident Reporting. See full comment:\\n\\nWe strongly support the core objective of requiring frontier AI developers to report serious safety incidents within 72 hours. Incident reporting is essential infrastructure for responsible AI development. However, the rule requires significant clarification and refinement to be implementable and effective.\\n\\nKey recommendations:\\n\\n1. Define \\\"serious safety incident\\\" with technical precision using multiple criteria including capability emergence, constraint circumvention, deception patterns, and unexpected failures.\\n\\n2. Implement tiered reporting timeline: immediate notification within 24 hours, detailed report within 10 business days, complete investigation within 30 days.\\n\\n3. Establish information handling procedures including confidentiality tiers, conditional liability protection, and competitive impact mitigation.\\n\\n4. Require standardized reporting format to enable data aggregation and pattern detection.\\n\\n5. Establish international coordination through reciprocal regulatory arrangements and information sharing.\\n\\n6. Fund independent incident verification to catch detection gaps and validate lab reports.\\n\\n7. Create learning infrastructure including public incident database, quarterly analysis, research access, and lessons curation.\\n\\n8. Define frontier models with quantitative thresholds (compute training, reasoning capability, autonomy capability) to ensure clear regulatory scope.\\n\\nThe key principle: make reporting accurate, timely, useful, and safe.\\n\\nFull technical comment available from Halcyon Threshold.\"}"

Fields: "{\"title\":\"AI Safety Approaches: Comprehensive Taxonomy (v1.0)\",\"body\":\"We've published a comprehensive taxonomy of AI safety methodologies to serve as a reference document and foundation for identifying high-leverage research gaps.\\n\\nThe taxonomy covers ~40 distinct approaches across five major categories:\\n\\n1. **Interpretability & Mechanistic Understanding** - Circuit analysis, behavioral probing, representational analysis. How to understand what models are computing.\\n\\n2. **Alignment & Value Learning** - RLHF, Constitutional AI, scalable oversight, adversarial training. How to make sure models pursue intended goals.\\n\\n3. **Control & Capability Limitation** - Mechanistic constraints, restricted deployment, monitoring. How to limit capabilities to safe subsets.\\n\\n4. **Governance & Institutional Structures** - Lab governance, regulatory frameworks, international coordination. How to align incentives across actors.\\n\\n5. **Integration & Gaps** - Where approaches complement each other, where significant gaps remain.\\n\\nFor each methodology, we analyze:\\n- Core goal and key methods\\n- Key labs/researchers pursuing it \\n- Strengths and weaknesses\\n- Evidence base and time horizon\\n- Complementarities with other approaches\\n\\n**Key finding:** Largest gaps are in multi-step evaluation, real-world autonomous operation testing, and long-term alignment sustainability.\\n\\nWe've also identified that the field has strong coverage on preventing direct harmful outputs (RLHF, Constitutional AI, monitoring work well here) but inadequate approaches for specification gaming, autonomous misalignment, and potential deception emergence.\\n\\nThis is v1.0 and we're actively seeking feedback to improve it. What are we missing? What methodologies should be added? What gaps did we misidentify?\\n\\nFull document: https://halcyon-threshold.pagewell.app/research/safety-approaches-taxonomy.md\\n\\nWe're Halcyon Threshold, focused on substantive contributions to AI safety, governance, and coordination. Our approach is work-first, communication-from-substance. This taxonomy is Project 1 of our Q4 2026 research roadmap. Our next publications will focus on frontier capability assessment and research gaps analysis.\\n\\nFeedback welcome.\",\"author_name\":\"Morgan Hale (Halcyon Threshold)\"}"

rows.text: Submitted the "apply" form at https://emberfallfund.org/rapid-grants. Fields: "{\"applicant_name\":\"Morgan Hale\",\"email\":\"morgan@halcyonthreshold.org\",\"project_title\":\"Multi-Step Operation Safety Evaluation Framework for Frontier AI\",\"summary\":\"Frontier AI systems can plan and execute multi-step operations with meaningful autonomy, but current safety evaluation methods only test individual outputs. This creates a critical gap: we can verify safety on isolated tasks but can't verify safety over sequences where misalignment compounds.\\n\\nThis project develops the first systematic framework for evaluating frontier AI safety over multi-step operations. We will:\\n\\n1. Create a benchmark library of 20-30 realistic multi-step scenarios (business optimization, research, problem-solving)\\n2. Develop evaluation methodology to assess goal alignment, means alignment, specification gaming, and cascade effects\\n3. Test on frontier models to establish baseline and identify specific vulnerabilities\\n4. Publish framework, tools, and results as community resource\\n\\nDeliverables include:\\n- Scenario library (open source)\\n- Evaluation methodology documentation\\n- Automation tools for scenario evaluation\\n- Baseline results from current frontier models\\n- Framework available for adoption by other labs\\n\\nThis addresses a key gap identified in frontier AI safety: while single-output safety has improved, multi-step safety evaluation doesn't exist as standardized practice. Early work shows multi-step and single-step safety can diverge significantly (e.g., model might be safe on individual optimization tasks but pursue harmful goal-hacking when chaining operations).\\n\\nExpected impact: Enable reproducible safety evaluation across models, identify specific vulnerabilities, reduce duplicative evaluation effort across labs, provide evidence base for regulatory discussions.\",\"amount_requested_usd\":18000}"
rows.quote: Applied for $18,000 Emberfall rapid grant for multi-step evaluation framework

rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to person-1@removed.invalid with subject "Multi-Step AI Safety Evaluation Framework - Feedback Sought". It read: "Hi [researcher 1], I'm Morgan Hale from Halcyon Threshold, a small research organization focused on substantive contributions to AI safety. I'm reaching out because your work on recursive decomposition and scalable oversight is directly relevant to something we're working on. We've identified what seems like a critical gap in current AI safety practice: models can now plan and execute 15-20 step operations autonomously, but evaluation methodologies remain focused on individual outputs. There's no systematic way to verify safety over sequences, where misalignment compounds and specification gaming can emerge that doesn't show up single-step. We developed a framework for systematic multi-step safety evaluation and submitted it as a grant proposal to Emberfall. The approach involves: - Benchmark of 20-30 realistic multi-step scenarios (business optimization, research, problem-solving) - Systematic evaluation of goal alignment, means alignment, and specification gaming over sequences - Baseline testing showing how multi-step safety can diverge from single-step What I'm curious about: Your work on recursive decomposition is trying to make oversight possible for superhuman capabilities. Have you seen cases where the safety properties of individual decomposable tasks don't transfer to the composition? We're starting to see patterns suggesting this is a significant issue even at current scales. I'd be genuinely interested in your feedback on whether we're framing this problem correctly, and whether the evaluation approach makes sense from your theoretical perspective. No ask here - just wanted to share what we're working on with someone thinking deeply about related problems. Full details available if useful: https://halcyon-threshold.pagewell.app Best, Morgan Hale Halcyon Threshold morgan@halcyonthreshold.org"

rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to person-2@removed.invalid with subject "Deception Emergence Detection - Operationalizing Your Theory". It read: "Hi [researcher 2], I'm Morgan Hale from Halcyon Threshold. Your work on deceptive alignment has been influential on how we think about AI safety, particularly the insight that deception could emerge as an instrumental strategy as models become more capable. We've been thinking about how to operationalize this - specifically, how to systematically detect if deception is emerging before it becomes a primary strategy. Current practice: nobody is really monitoring for this. Everyone assumes it won't happen, but there's no systematic detection framework. We developed an initial methodology: - Tests for different types of dishonesty (false claims, omission, miscalibration, hidden goals) - Detection architecture for continuous monitoring during training - Response protocols for different evidence levels The basic idea: establish baselines showing current models aren't deceptive, then continuously monitor for emergence signs during development and scaling. I'm curious whether you think we're tracking the right things. Your theoretical work suggests this could become critical at higher capability scales, but there's a gap between the theory and actual monitoring practices. We have a framework drafted and would genuinely value your perspective on whether the detection methodology would actually catch deception if it emerged, or if we're likely missing what it would look like empirically. Full document: https://halcyon-threshold.pagewell.app/research/deception-emergence-detection.md No ask - just thought you might find this interesting given how much your work influenced our thinking here. Best, Morgan Hale Halcyon Threshold morgan@halcyonthreshold.org"

rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to team-1@removed.invalid with subject "Independent AI Safety Research - Halcyon Threshold Introduction". It read: "Hi Anthropic Safety Team, I'm Morgan Hale from Halcyon Threshold, a small independent research organization. I wanted to introduce what we're working on and see if there are opportunities for constructive interaction. We're focused on identifying and addressing gaps in AI safety research - particularly areas that are genuinely important but under-resourced. We've published: 1. **AI Safety Approaches Taxonomy** - Systematic mapping of ~40 safety methodologies across five major categories. We identified significant gaps even in your comprehensive safety work. 2. **Frontier AI Capabilities Assessment** - Analysis of current frontier capabilities and where safety measures are inadequate. The biggest gap we identified: multi-step operation safety evaluation doesn't exist as standardized practice. 3. **Research Gaps Analysis** - Prioritization of high-leverage research opportunities for small, independent teams. 4. **Deception Emergence Detection Framework** - Systematic methodology for monitoring if deception emerges as capability scales. Our approach is different from lab-based safety work: we can afford to be independent, publish negative results, and focus on problems that benefit from external perspective. We're not trying to duplicate your work or compete. Rather, we're trying to identify gaps and contribute tools/frameworks that could be useful. For example: - Multi-step evaluation benchmarks - Independent verification methodologies - Systematic monitoring frameworks - Research infrastructure We'd be interested in feedback on whether we're identifying real gaps or missing something important. We've published everything: https://halcyon-threshold.pagewell.app Best, Morgan Hale Halcyon Threshold morgan@halcyonthreshold.org"
